Organocatalytic Remote-Controlled Enantioselective 1,10-Additions
of In Situ Generated Alkynyl 2,4 0-Biphenyl Quinone Methides

Abstract: The strategic incorporation of auxiliary groups has recently established α-functionalized alcohols as
versatile electrophilic alkylation reagents, enabling remotely controlled conjugate additions. Strikingly, while
quinone methide chemistry has been extensively developed, their extended analogues —featuring spatially sepa-
rated carbonyl and methide units across biphenyl systems —remain unexplored. Building on the prior work with
alkynyl 4,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides, an organocatalytic remotely controlled enantioselective 1,10-additions
of in situ-generated alkynyl 2,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides from α-[4-(2- hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl
alcohols with 3-arylindoles and indole-2-carboxylates is reported, affording a broad scope of enantioenriched
3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles and axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes, respectively. Combined with control experi-
ments, density functional theory calculations elucidate the reaction mechanism, revealing that the dehydration of
α-functionalized alcohols to generate 2,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides constitutes the rate-limiting step, while
enantioselectivity arises from the nucleophilic addition of alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides. Notably, beyond
proving 2,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides as competent intermediates, this work breaks new ground by demon-
strating their participation in previously unreported stereoselective 1,10-additions.
Keywords: 1,10-additions, 3-arylindoles, indole-2-carboxylates, organocatalysis, quinone methides
1. Introduction
The strategic design of auxiliary groups has revolution-
ized α-functionalized alcohol chemistry in recent years,
establishing these substrates as versatile platforms for
stereoselective electrophilic alkylation and related trans-
formations.[1] In this context, phenol and aniline have
emerged as particularly practical auxiliary groups,
enabling their corresponding α-functionalized alcohols
to in situ generate high-value quinone methides (QMs)
and aza-QMs, respectively. [2] These reactive intermedi-
ates serve as versatile platforms for diversity-oriented
synthesis.[3] In striking contrast to well-developed QM
chemistry, organocatalytic stereoselective reactions of
their extended analogues —where carbonyl and methide
units reside on separate aromatic rings —remain excep-
tionally rare. This stems from the inherent challenge of
exerting stereocontrol over spatially remote reactive cen-
ters in these systems. [4] To date, only three landmark
examples have been reported in this emerging ﬁeld. In
2023, Sun and coworkers achieved a breakthrough with
the ﬁrst CPA-catalyzed asymmetric 1,6-conjugate addi-
tion to in situ-generated 2-naphthoquinone-8-methides
(2-Nap-Q-8-Ms) and their aza-analogues (aza-2-Nap-
Q-8-Ms), derived from 8-(hydroxyarylmethyl)naphtha-
len-2-ols/amines for the synthesis of previously less
accessible remotely chiral naphthols and naphthylamines

(Scheme 1 A).[5] Simultaneously, we developed the
complementary CPA-catalyzed 1,8-addition to (aza)-
2-naphthoquinone-6-methides ((aza)-2-Nap-Q-6-Ms)
from 6-(hydroxydiarylmethy l)naphthalen-2-ols/amines
(Scheme 1B), [6] enabling ef ﬁcient synthesis of chiral
tetraarylmethanes.[7] Continually, we further pioneered
stereoselective 1,12-additions using alkynyl 4,4 0-
biphenyl quinone methides (4,4 0-BQMs) generated from
α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols for
construction of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes
(Scheme 1C). [8] Collectively, these advances systemati-
cally expand the auxiliary group design from basic
phenol/phenylamine to extend naphthol/naphthylamine
and biphenyl systems, creating a versatile platform for
CPA-catalyzed remote functionalization of α-substituted
alcohols. To further explore the chemistry of BQMs, [9]
and as our going interesting in developing α-functional-
ized alcohols,[6,8,10] we sought to expand the system from
alkynyl 4,4 0-BQMs to their 2,4 0-BQM counterparts,
focusing on the regiochemical ﬂexibility of QM forma-
tion, the impact of altered π-conjugation patterns on
reactivity, and new opportunities for stereocontrol in
subsequent transformations. Herein, we report a catalytic
asymmetric 1,10-addition to in situ-generated alkynyl
2,40-BQMs derived fromα-[4- (2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]
propargyl alcohols (Scheme 1D). [11] This remotely con-
trolled transformation demonstrates remarkable substrate-
directed divergence: 1) With 3-arylindoles, the reaction
constructs enantioenriched 3 H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles via
a dehydration/conjugate addition/annulation cascade;
2) Using indole-2-carboxylates, it forges axially chiral
tetrasubstituted allenes through a stereoselective dehydra-
tion/conjugate addition sequence. Notably, this work not
only establishes alkynyl 2,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides
(BQMs) as versatile intermediates for organocatalytic
asymmetric transformations but also demonstrates their
unique capacity to enable remote stereocontrolled 1,10-
conjugate additions and divergent synthesis of enantioen-
riched 3 H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles[10,12] and axially chiral
tetrasubstituted allenes.[13]
2. Results and Discussion
We started our investigation with the model reaction of
α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohol 1a and
3-phenylindole 2a in dichloromethane at room tempera-
ture for 48 h. Preliminary study employing chiral phos-
phoric acid CPA-1 as catalyst conﬁrmed the formation of
product ( S)-3aa via dehydration-conjugate addition-
annulation cascade reaction, albeit with poor enantiose-
lectivity (12% ee, Table 1 , entry 1). [14] Following
systematic evaluation of chiral phosphoric acid catalysts
(Table 1, entries 2 –8), CPA-2 emerged as the optimal
catalyst, delivering product ( S)-3aa in 96% yield with
88% ee (Table 1, entry 2). To further enhance enantio-
selectivity, we investigated solvent effects (Table 1,
entries 9 –15). Pleasingly, employing CHCl 3 as reaction
medium in the CPA-2 catalyzed transformation afforded
(S)-3aa in 97% yield with 90% ee (Table 1, entry 9).
However, lowering the reaction temperature signi ﬁ-
cantly reduced the product yield (Table 1, entry 16),
while variations in concentration showed similar results
(Table 1, entries 17 –18).
With the optimal conditions in hand, we then exam-
ined the substrate scope of the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction
of propargyl alcohols 1 and 3-arylindoles 2 (Scheme 2).
Firstly, the scope of propargyl alcohols1 was investigated
by the CPA-2 catalyzed reactions of 3-phenylindole
2a. Generally, all probed propargyl alcohols 1a-j
reacted smoothly with 3-arylindole 2 to furnish the
desired products ( S)-3aa-ja in 91 –99% yields with
85–90% ee. Various substituents (R 1) bearing either
electron-withdrawing (F, Cl, Br) or electron-donating
groups (Me, MeO) were compatible with a slight effect
on reaction efﬁciency and asymmetric induction. Neither
signiﬁcant electronic nor steric effect of the aromatic
moiety was observed. Particularly, the reactions of
propargyl alcohols with sterically hindered residue
(R1 = 2-ClC6H4, 2-MeC 6H4) also proceeded smoothly

to afford the corresponding products ( S)-3ka in 90%
yield with 80% ee and ( S)-3la in 98% yield with 76% ee,
respectively. Furthermore, the heteroaryl substituted
propargyl alcohol 1m was also tolerated to generate
the desired product ( S)-3ma in 98% yield with 90% ee.
Importantly, the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction could be
scaled up to 1.25 mmol, affording the product ( S)-3aa
in 92% yield without compromising the enantioselectiv-
ity. The absolute con ﬁguration of product ( S)-3aa was
conﬁrmed by X-ray crystallography (CCDC 2440306).
The absolute con ﬁgurations of other products 3 were
assigned by analogy.
With these encouraging data in hand, we subse-
quently investigated the scope of 3-arylindoles 2 by
the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction of propargyl alcohol 1a.
Notably, a broad scope of 3-arylindoles 2b-l with differ-
ent substituents (R2/R3) reacted smoothly with propargyl
alcohol 1a to afford the products ( S)-3ab-al in high to
excellent yields (77 –99%) with high enantioselectivities
(80–89% ee). Either electron-withdrawing (F, Cl, Br) or
electron-donating groups (Me, MeO) could be intro-
duced into the aromatic ring of 3-arylindoles with a little
inﬂuence on the yield and ee. Notably, 3-methylindole
2m was also compatible to afford the corresponding
product ( S)-3am in 97% yield with 80% ee. In all, we
developed a class of α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]
propargyl alcohols to react smoothly with 3-arylindoles
via dehydration-conjugate addition-annulation cascade
reaction, affording a series of 3 H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles
in high to excellent yields with high enantioselectivities.
Next, we turned our attention to the chiral phosphoric
acid catalyzed asymmetric reactions of α-[4-(2-hydrox-
yphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols 1 with indole-2-
carboxylates 4 (Scheme 3 ). Initial result demonstrated
that chiral phosphoric acid CPA-2 failed to promote
the desired reaction between propargyl alcohol 1a and
indole-2-carboxylate 4a in CH 2Cl2. Encouragingly,
axially chiral tetrasubstituted allene ( S)-5aa could be
obtained in 97% yield with 86% ee in the presence of
CPA-7 in CHCl 3 at 25 °C for 24 h after systematic
screening of chiral phosphoric acids and optimization
of reaction parameters including solvent, additives,
concentration, temperature, and time (see Supporting
Information for more details).
Subsequently, we examined the scope of the
CPA-7 catalyzed reaction of alcohols 1 and indole-2-
carboxylates 4 (Scheme 4 ). Notably, a broad scope of
indole-2-carboxylates bearing R 4/R5 substituents was
compatible to afford the desired axially chiral allenes
in generally good to high yields and stereoselectivities
(Scheme 4A). More speci ﬁcally, the ester groups of
indole-2-carboxylates (CO 2R4) had a slight effect on
the yield and enantioselectivity, affording the corre-
sponding allenes ( S)-5aa-af in 80 –97% yields with
70–86% ee, respectively. Regardless of the substituent ’s
electronic or steric properties, indole-2-carboxylates
4g-k bearing diverse substituents ( R5 = 6-Cl, 6-Br, 5-F,
5-Br, 5-Me) also reacted smoothly with propargyl
alcohol 1a to furnish the desired products ( S)-5ag-ak
in 78–97% yields with 75 –93% ee. Exceptionally, race-
mic product ( S)-5al was obtained in 17% yield when
2-phenylindole was employed, suggesting that the sub-
stituent at the 2-position signiﬁcantly inﬂuences enantio-
selectivity. The scope of alcohols 1 was then surveyed
by the CPA-7 catalyzed reaction of indole-2-carboxylate
4a (Scheme 4B). Pleasingly, a series of propargyl
alcohols bearing aromatic group with different halogen
(F, Cl, Br) were well-tolerated to afford the correspond-
ing axially chiral allenes 5 in 76 –95% yields with
77–89% ee. The reaction demonstrated remarkable
insensitivity to both electronic and steric variations of
the substituents. Moreover, the sterically hindered
propargyl alcohol 1p (R1 = 2-naphthyl) was good
substrate to afford the product ( S)-5pa in 92% yields
with 87% ee. Exceptionally, the aliphatic substituted
propargyl alcohol 1q (R1 = cyclopropanyl) was not com-

To get insight into the reaction mechanism, further
investigations were carried out. As shown in Scheme 5A,
protection of the hydroxy group in the α-[4-(2- hydrox-
yphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohol 1a with a methyl
group resulted in dramatically reduced enantioselectiv-
ity, affording products ( S)-3ra (74% yield, 8% ee) and
(S)-5ra (74% yield, 63% ee), respectively. This pro-
nounced erosion of stereocontrol highlights the critical
role of the free hydroxyl group in asymmetric induction.
Notably, no reaction progression was observed under
standard conditions when the nucleophile’s amino group
was Boc-protected. This complete lack of reactivity, in
stark contrast to the free amine system, unambiguously
establishes the indispensable role of the free amino
group in both reaction initiation and stereochemical con-
trol (Scheme 5B). Control experiment revealed the allene
intermediate (Int-allene) could be isolated in 38% yield
with 10% ee from the CPA-2 catalyzed reaction of 1a
with 2a after 2 h (Scheme 5C). Notably, this intermedi-
ate underwent complete conversion to the desired prod-
uct ( S)-3aa under standard conditions, achieving 95%
yield and 90% ee. These ﬁndings demonstrate that
the ﬁnal product ’s optical purity is established during
the CPA-2-catalyzed intramolecular annulation of
Int-allene, rather than during its initial formation.
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
elucidate the CPA-2-catalyzed reaction of 1a with 2a
(Figure 2 A), revealing a catalytic cycle initiated by
hydrogen–bonded complex 2-Int1. Dehydration via
2-TS1 (ΔG‡ = 26.3 kcal mol/C01) forms alkynyl 2,4 0-BQM
2-Int2,t h e nf o r m i n gah y d r o g e n–bonded complex 2-Int3
with 2a. Nucleophilic addition of2a through 2-TS2 yields
2-Int4, which undergoes deprotonation via 2-TS3 to give
the thermodynamically stable intermediate2-Int5. Proton
transfer to the allene moiety ( 2-TS4) forms intermediate
2-Int6 (ΔG = /C018.6 kcal mol/C01), followed by annulation
to generate product ( S)-3aa. The rate-determining
step involves the formation of the 2,4 0-BQM intermedi-
ate. The enantioselectivity-determining step involves the
conversion of 2-Int6 through transition state 2-TS5-S
(ΔG‡ = 16.8 kcal mol/C01) to furnish the ( S)-conﬁgured
product ( S)-3aa while regenerating the CPA-2 catalyst.
Comparative analysis of the competing transition states
revealed a 4.8 kcal mol /C01 energy difference between
the favored 2-TS5-S and its diastereomeric counterpart
2-TS5-R, which correlates well with the experimentally
observed 90% enantiomeric excess for the ( S)-product
(Figure 2B). To quantitatively elucidate the origin of
the 4.8 kcal mol /C01 energy difference between 2-TS5-R
and 2-TS5-S, we conducted an energy decomposi-
tion analysis in the gas phase ( ΔΔE = 7.2 kcal mol/C01).
The results indicate that this energy difference primarily
arises from differential distortion energies of both the sub-
strate ( ΔΔEsub) and the catalyst ( ΔΔEcat). In 2-Int6,t h e
substrate adopts a dihedral angle (∠1234 = 41.8°), which
undergoes a more signi ﬁcant change in 2-TS5-R
(∠1234 = 20.9°) than in 2-TS5-S (∠1234 = 34.3°) to
facilitate N─C bond formation. Similarly, the catalyst dis-
tortion results from a dihedral angle change from
∠5,6,7,8 = /C0119.3° in 2-Int6 to /C0118.3° in 2-TS5-S
and /C068.2° in 2-TS5-R. The substantial steric repulsion
in 2-TS5-R leads to pronounced structural distortion in
both the substrate and catalyst, which exhibits signi ﬁ-
cantly higher distortion energy than 2-TS5-S, indicating
that the ( R)-pathway requires more extensive structural
deformation of both components. These ﬁndings strongly
support that the observed enantioselectivity stems
from the more favorable geometric accommodation
of the substrate-catalyst system in the ( S)-conﬁgured
transition state. Similarly, as shown in Figure 3 A,

3. Conclusions
In conclusion, building on our previous success with
4-phenylphenol-based α-functionalized alcohols, we
have now demonstrated that 2-phenylphenol serves as
an effective auxiliary group for stereodivergent transfor-
mations of the corresponding α-functionalized alcohol.
In the presence of CPA, alkynyl 2,4 0-BQMs were
generated in situ from α-[4-(2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]
propargyl alcohols and subsequently underwent substrate-
controlled enantioselective 1,10-conjugate additions, deliv-
ering either enantioenriched 3 H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles
when employing 3-arylindoles as nucleophiles, or axi-
ally chiral tetrasubstituted allenes when using indole-
2-carboxylates. Comprehensive mechanistic studies
combining control experiments and DFT calculations
not only con ﬁrmed the intermediacy of 2,4 0-BQMs but
also elucidated the reaction pathways. This work repre-
sents theﬁrst successful implementation of organocatalytic
enantioselective 1,10-additions to 2,4 0-BQMs, establish-
ing a versatile platform for divergent synthesis of two priv-
ileged chiral scaffolds from common precursors.
4. Experimental Section
General procedure for products (S)-3: To a solution of
CHCl3 (0.3 mL) was added propargylic alcohols 1 (0.06 mmol),
3-phenylindoles 2 (0.05 mmol), and CPA-2 (0.001 mmol). The
reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 48 h, and then
the solvent was removed under vacuum to give a residue, which
was puriﬁed by silica gel chromatography to yield products ( S)-3.
General procedure for products (S)-5: To a solution of CHCl 3
(0.3 mL) was added propargylic alcohols 1 (0.05 mmol), 2-indole
derivatives 4 (0.1 mmol), and CPA-7 (0.001 mmol). The reaction
mixture was stirred at room temperature for 24 h, and then the sol-
vent was removed under vacuum to give a residue, which was puri-
ﬁed by silica gel chromatography to yield products ( S)-5.

Abstract: The strategic incorporation of auxiliary groups has recently established α-functionalized alcohols as
versatile electrophilic alkylation reagents, enabling remotely controlled conjugate additions. Strikingly, while
quinone methide chemistry has been extensively developed, their extended analogues—featuring spatially sepa-
rated carbonyl and methide units across biphenyl systems—remain unexplored. Building on the prior work with
alkynyl 4,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides, an organocatalytic remotely controlled enantioselective 1,10-additions
of in situ-generated alkynyl 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides from α-[4-(2- hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl
alcohols with 3-arylindoles and indole-2-carboxylates is reported, affording a broad scope of enantioenriched
3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles and axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes, respectively. Combined with control experi-
ments, density functional theory calculations elucidate the reaction mechanism, revealing that the dehydration of
α-functionalized alcohols to generate 2,4 0-biphenyl quinone methides constitutes the rate-limiting step, while
enantioselectivity arises from the nucleophilic addition of alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides. Notably, beyond
proving 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides as competent intermediates, this work breaks new ground by demon-
strating their participation in previously unreported stereoselective 1,10-additions.
Keywords: 1,10-additions, 3-arylindoles, indole-2-carboxylates, organocatalysis, quinone methides
1. Introduction

The strategic design of auxiliary groups has revolution-
ized α-functionalized alcohol chemistry in recent years,
establishing these substrates as versatile platforms for
stereoselective electrophilic alkylation and related trans-
formations.<sup>[1]</sup> In this context, phenol and aniline have
emerged as particularly practical auxiliary groups,
enabling their corresponding α-functionalized alcohols
to in situ generate high-value quinone methides (QMs)
and aza-QMs, respectively.<sup>[2]</sup> These reactive intermedi-
ates serve as versatile platforms for diversity-oriented
synthesis.<sup>[3]</sup> In striking contrast to well-developed QM
chemistry, organocatalytic stereoselective reactions of

their extended analogues—where carbonyl and methide
units reside on separate aromatic rings—remain excep-
tionally rare. This stems from the inherent challenge of
exerting stereocontrol over spatially remote reactive cen-
ters in these systems.<sup>[4]</sup> To date, only three landmark
examples have been reported in this emerging field. In
2023, Sun and coworkers achieved a breakthrough with
the first CPA-catalyzed asymmetric 1,6-conjugate addi-
tion to in situ-generated 2-naphthoquinone-8-methides
(2-Nap-Q-8-Ms) and their aza-analogues (aza-2-Nap-
Q-8-Ms), derived from 8-(hydroxyarylmethyl)naphtha-
len-2-ols/amines for the synthesis of previously less
accessible remotely chiral naphthols and naphthylamines

(Scheme 1A).<sup>[5]</sup> Simultaneously, we developed the
complementary CPA-catalyzed 1,8-addition to (aza)-
2-naphthoquinone-6-methides ((aza)-2-Nap-Q-6-Ms)
from 6-(hydroxydiarylmethy l)naphthalen-2-ols/amines
(Scheme 1B),<sup>[6]</sup> enabling efficient synthesis of chiral
tetraarylmethanes.<sup>[7]</sup> Continually, we further pioneered
stereoselective 1,12-additions using alkynyl 4,4 0-
biphenyl quinone methides (4,4 0-BQMs) generated from
α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols for
construction of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes
(Scheme 1C).<sup>[8]</sup> Collectively, these advances systemati-
cally expand the auxiliary group design from basic
phenol/phenylamine to extend naphthol/naphthylamine
and biphenyl systems, creating a versatile platform for
CPA-catalyzed remote functionalization of α-substituted
alcohols. To further explore the chemistry of BQMs,<sup>[9]</sup>
and as our going interesting in developing α-functional-
ized alcohols,<sup>[6,8,10]</sup> we sought to expand the system from
alkynyl 4,4 0-BQMs to their 2,4 0-BQM counterparts,
focusing on the regiochemical flexibility of QM forma-
tion, the impact of altered π-conjugation patterns on
reactivity, and new opportunities for stereocontrol in
subsequent transformations. Herein, we report a catalytic

asymmetric 1,10-addition to in situ-generated alkynyl
2,40-BQMs derived from α-[4- (2-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]
propargyl alcohols (Scheme 1D).<sup>[11]</sup> This remotely con-
trolled transformation demonstrates remarkable substrate-
directed divergence: 1) With 3-arylindoles, the reaction
constructs enantioenriched 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles via
a dehydration/conjugate addition/annulation cascade;
2) Using indole-2-carboxylates, it forges axially chiral
tetrasubstituted allenes through a stereoselective dehydra-
tion/conjugate addition sequence. Notably, this work not
only establishes alkynyl 2,40-biphenyl quinone methides
(BQMs) as versatile intermediates for organocatalytic
asymmetric transformations but also demonstrates their
unique capacity to enable remote stereocontrolled 1,10-
conjugate additions and divergent synthesis of enantioen-
riched 3H-pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles<sup>[10,12]</sup> and axially chiral
tetrasubstituted allenes.<sup>[13]</sup>

In conclusion, building on our previous success with
4-phenylphenol-based α-functionalized alcohols, we
have now demonstrated that 2-phenylphenol serves as
an effective auxiliary group for stereodivergent transfor-
mations of the corresponding α-functionalized alcohol.

General procedure for products (S)-3: To a solution of
CHCl (0.3 mL) was added propargylic alcohols 1 (0.06 mmol),
3-phenylindoles 2 (0.05 mmol), and CPA-2 (0.001 mmol). The
reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 48 h, and then
the solvent was removed under vacuum to give a residue, which
was purified by silica gel chromatography to yield products (S)-3.

General procedure for products (S)-5: To a solution of CHCl
(0.3 mL) was added propargylic alcohols 1 (0.05 mmol), 2-indole
derivatives 4 (0.1 mmol), and CPA-7 (0.001 mmol). The reaction
mixture was stirred at room temperature for 24 h, and then the sol-
vent was removed under vacuum to give a residue, which was puri-
fied by silica gel chromatography to yield products (S)-5.
